newsitem.title: SENEGAL: Hillary Clinton leaves Senegal for South Africa.
newsitem.headline: Hillary Clinton leaves Senegal for South Africa.

text.p: U.S. first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton and her daughter Chelsea left Senegal for South Africa on Monday after kicking off a six-nation Africa tour with a visit to the former slave island of Goree, witnesses said.

Mrs Clinton, who will also visit Zimbabwe, Uganda, Tanzania and Eritrea, described Goree Island, one of the departure points for African slaves shipped to the Americas, as "one of the most heartbreaking monuments of anywhere in the world".
Hillary Clinton and her daughter took an overnight flight to Johannesburg, South Africa, second leg of a two-week tour of Africa.

Mrs Clinton and Chelsea started their tour of Africa by visiting Goree Island off the coast of Senegal, one of many coastal enclaves on Africa's western bulge where European slave traders processed millions of Africans captured for a life of slavery in North and South America.

The first lady and 17-year-old Chelsea took a 15-minute ferry ride to Goree Island, where curator Joseph Ndiaye showed them the gloomy rooms that slaves were crammed into before they were herded out the "Door of No Return" onto ships that took them away from their homeland.
Above the door is written the inscription: "Door of No Return. From this door for a voyage without return. They went, their eyes fixed on the infinity of suffering."
"I just can't imagine what it would be like," Mrs Clinton said after touching the stone in the shadowy hallway leading to the Atlantic Ocean beyond.

Ndiaye told that slavery flourished for 300 years on Goree until it was outlawed by France in 1848. He said Many African-Americans come to Goree looking for clues to their misty past and that he tells them: "It was the finest race that left here because they were selected."
"That door represents nothing less that the depths of human depravity," Mrs Clinton said later in a visit to the Martin Luther King School for Girls, named for the slain American civil rights leader.

Part of the trip was an hour inland drove to the village of Saam Njaay, a dusty community of thatched huts and clay ovens where the democratic spirit of neighbour helping neighbour is straight out of the pages of Mrs Clinton's book, "It Takes a Village".
The first lady danced with villagers in brightly coloured costumes and heard appeals to help the region's villages be connected with roads and electricity.

The village of 300 people showed its respect by bestowing African names on her and Chelsea. Mrs Clinton may now also be known as Ayda Njaay, chosen because a village teacher with the same name shares Mrs Clinton's outspoken attitude.
Chelsea was given the name Aissatou Toure.
Before leaving Senegal, Mrs Clinton paid a visit to that West African country's president Abdou Diouf.
